To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the neurons of the brain stem and posterior thalamic nuclei respond to genital, somatic, and nociception stimulation in the squirrel monkeys, and that these neurons display species typical characteristics.

(1) the brain stem and posterior thalamic neurons responding to genital stimulation in the monkey have properties that parallel those of the neurons responding to genital and somatosensory stimulation in the rat and cat; (2) the brain stem neurons responding to genital stimuli in the monkey are widely distributed in the caudal brain stem, and the posterior thalamus; (3) genital, somatosensitive, and nociceptively responsive neurons are not distributed at random in the brain stem

neurons in the brain stem and posterior thalamus are responsive to a variety of genital stimuli, including vaginal probing, cervical stimulation, and touch-pressure and nociceptive stimuli applied to the perineal region.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the study of brain stem neuronal mechanisms involved in the processing of genital and nociceptive sensory information.
the neural basis of sexual behavior.
the neural mechanisms underlying genital behavior in primates.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the neurons in this area of the brain stem and posterior thalamus are not organized into separate, discrete, anatomically distinct, and functionally specific sensory systems, but rather that they represent a continuum of neurons which are responsive to a variety of sensory modalities and which are organized into functional groups based on the convergence of their receptive fields.

the brain stem and posterior thalamic neurons responding to genital and somatic stimuli are not organized into discrete functional groups, but rather are a heterogeneous population with a variety of response properties and sensory convergence.
the brain stem and posterior thalamic neurons studied in this investigation are part of an extensive, widely distributed, and highly responsive sensory system.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the neurons studied are involved in a complex, multisensory, sensory-motor integration of information for genital and somatosensory stimuli.

the brain stem and posterior thalamic nuclei are the sites of convergence of genital, somatic, and nociceptor inputs, and that the cells there are capable of processing information about these inputs in a complex manner.
genital sensory information is processed in the monkey brain stem and diencephalon in a manner similar to the processing of somatosensory information from other body regions.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the brain stem is a very important site of integration of sensory input from the genital tract and other sensory modalities.
the brain stem tegmental and posterior dience phalic neurons have the potential to play important roles in the control of genital reflexes and genital sensory perception.

the brain stem tegmental region is a rich source of cells responding to genital, recto-genital, and somatosensory stimulation and that the response properties of these cells have parallels to those of cells in other species.
